claims.text: The nanoparticles are equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Oxide surface modification influences the stability of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Oxide coating affects elemental segregation in the nanoparticles.
Oxide coating alters interfacial effects in the nanoparticles.
Oxide coating affects elemental diffusion in the nanoparticles.
Changes in segregation, interface effects, and elemental diffusion affect secondary-phase formation.
Secondary-phase formation and the proposed interfacial and diffusional effects determine overall nanoparticle stability.
Coatings thinner than 2 nm will reduce nanoparticle stability relative to the initial unmodified baseline.
Coatings thinner than 2 nm will increase elemental segregation.
Coatings thinner than 2 nm will increase secondary-phase formation.
Coatings thicker than 3 nm will maintain nanoparticle stability relative to the initial unmodified baseline.
The stability associated with coatings thicker than 3 nm results from a protective oxide-layer effect.
The proposed comparison varies oxide-coating thickness from 1 to 5 nm and thermal treatment from 473 to 1923 K under an inert atmosphere.
The prediction is intended to apply during temperature cycling under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions over 473–1923 K.

contradictions.description: The prediction defines thinner coatings as less than 2 nm and thicker coatings as greater than 3 nm, whereas the falsification rule labels coatings greater than 2 nm as thinner and coatings less than 3 nm as thicker. These reversed and overlapping classifications make the stated falsification ranges internally inconsistent.
